newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir hostages' families to seek Pakistani help.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir hostages' families to seek Pakistani help.

text.p: The families of two Britons abducted nearly two years ago in Kashmir said on Thursday they would seek help from Pakistan's intelligence service, Moslem leaders and government officials in finding their loved ones.

"We hope to be able to make an appeal at the main mosque in Muzaffarabad," said Bob Wells, father of hostage Paul Wells. He was referring to the capital city of the one third of Kashmir that Pakistan controls.
Wells, who was due to arrive in Pakistan on Friday, said he would also ask the government's Inter Services Intelligence wing to conduct a search for the hostages.

Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan were abducted by Al-Faran guerrillas in July 1995 while trekking in Kashmir. German Dirk Hasert, Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe and Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs were also captured.
Childs escaped but Ostroe was later found beheaded. There has been no trace of the other four for 16 months, raising doubts over whether they are still alive.

Wells was accompanied by his son's girlfriend, Catherine Moseley, Mangan's wife, Julie, and a cousin of hers. They have already met senior Indian police and government officials, Kashmiri separatist leaders and Red Cross representatives.

The four Britons also planned to meet representatives of the Harkat-ul-Ansar guerrilla group in Pakistan. Indian authorities and foreign missions say the group backed the kidnapping of the Westerners by the shadowy Al-Faran guerrilla group.
Harkat-ul-Ansar denies any ties with Al-Faran and last week issued its own appeal for the hostages' release.

"The crucial call for us in Pakistan will be on the Harkat-ul-Ansar," Wells told a news conference. "They have got to stand up and send people into the (Kashmir) Valley to get information. It is the least they can do."
Asked to comment on reports that Israeli psychic Uri Geller had offered to help free the hostages, Mangan said: "We would be grateful for any help we can get from anyone."

"Our boys came as innocent tourists. We just want to take them home," she said. "If they are dead, God forbid, we still want to take them home, we have our own customs. If they are alive, all we want is a photograph or some other proof. It is just getting more difficult for us, day by day."
